tagline: Across Grayback summit to the Klamath and a proposed state’s capital
intro: The State of Jefferson Scenic Byway links O’Brien, Oregon, and Yreka, California, by way of the 5,000-foot Grayback summit and the Klamath River. The drive covers 108 miles through old spruce forests and along the river, with two hours and 40 minutes allowed without stops. The Forest Service includes it among the three scenic byways through Klamath National Forest. Seiad Valley brings another feature into the river journey: the three craggy Lower Devils peaks overlook a forested valley enclosed by the Klamath Mountains.

Yreka’s claim to state-capital status belongs to a short-lived secession movement. On November 27, 1941, young men carrying hunting rifles stopped traffic on US 99 south of town and distributed a proclamation of independence from California and Oregon. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, supporters turned their efforts toward the war, weakening the movement. The proclamation promised to “secede every Thursday until further notice.” John Leon Childs was inaugurated as the proposed state’s governor on December 4, 1941.

Traveling from Oregon, leave US 199 at O’Brien and cross Grayback through the spruce forests toward Indian Creek and Happy Camp. There the drive joins Highway 96 along the Klamath. Follow it east toward Highway 263, then head south across the five Pioneer bridges to Yreka.

moments.title: O'Brien
moments.text: At O’Brien, the byway meets US 199 in the valley of the West Fork Illinois River. The river flows north toward the Rogue, while US 199 connects the community with Cave Junction to the north and the California line five miles south. The town’s small group of businesses stands at Redwood Highway and Lone Mountain Road. East of O’Brien lie Waldo, now a ghost town, and then Takilma. Waldo began in 1852 as the gold-mining camp Sailor’s Diggings and became Josephine County’s first county seat. Its post office closed in 1928.

moments.title: Happy Camp
moments.text: Happy Camp sits where the Klamath meets a network of creeks, including Indian Creek and Elk Creek. It is the byway’s junction between Highway 96 and the road over Grayback to Oregon. Gold-rush miners gave the town its name. H. C. Chester, who interviewed Jack Titus in 1882–83, credited Titus with naming it after his partner James Camp’s delighted arrival. The Karuk Tribe is headquartered here, as are the Happy Camp/Oak Knoll Ranger Districts of Klamath National Forest. Another early reference comes from Redick McKee, who recorded “Mr Roache’s Happy Camp” at Murderer’s Bar on November 8, 1851.

moments.title: Seiad Valley
moments.text: Three craggy peaks called the Lower Devils overlook Seiad Valley, a forested valley enclosed by the Klamath Mountains. Homes cluster along the Klamath River, Highway 96 and the surrounding creeks. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the valley’s west side. The proposed State of Jefferson has a visible emblem here: its flag flies over the general store. Over the nearby elementary school flies the American flag. In spring and summer, hikers passing through to buy supplies are a frequent sight in the central area. Seiad Day brings an annual parade and music.
moments.notice: The Lower Devils’ three craggy peaks overlook the forested valley.

practical: O'Brien: The road over Grey Back Pass is seasonal and is not cleared or maintained in snow. The Forest Service in Happy Camp provides closure information. (checked 2026-10-11)
